cards.q: Rolling a fair die 20 times. How many 6s do you get?
cards.note: Fixed number of independent trials, two outcomes (6 / not-6), constant p.

cards.q: Emails arriving in a fixed hour. Rare, independent, can cluster.
cards.note: Count of rare independent events in a fixed interval.

cards.q: Flipping a coin until the first head appears. How many flips?
cards.note: Number of independent trials up to (and including) the first success.

cards.q: Number of defective items in a batch of 50, with a fixed defect rate.
cards.note: n = 50 fixed trials, each item defective or not, constant probability.

cards.q: The success probability in a Binomial
cards.a: Probability of success on each single trial.
cards.note: Near 0 → successes rare; p = 0.5 → symmetric distribution.

cards.q: The rate parameter of a Poisson
cards.a: Expected count per unit time or space.
cards.note: Emails average 3/hr → λ = 3. Higher λ = expect more events.

cards.q: Mean and variance of a Binomial(n, p)
cards.note: As p → 0 the variance shrinks — fewer successes overall.

cards.q: Mean and variance of a Poisson(λ)
cards.note: Mean equals variance — a Poisson fingerprint. If Var ≫ mean, it's overdispersed.

cards.q: Mean of a Geometric — trials until the first success (p)
cards.note: p = 0.2 → expect 5 trials. Rarer success = longer wait.

cards.q: For a Poisson(λ), the probability of zero events
cards.note: λ = 2 → P(0) ≈ 0.135. Not zero: rare events often just don't happen.

cards.q: "Can I use a Poisson approximation to a Binomial with n = 20, p = 0.4?"
cards.note: Poisson approximates Binomial when n is large and p is small (np stays moderate).

cards.q: What four conditions must hold to call something Binomial?
cards.a: Fixed n, independent trials, two outcomes, constant p.
cards.note: Break any one — e.g. p drifts, or trials interact — and it isn't Binomial.

cards.q: Why is the Geometric distribution called memoryless?
cards.a: Past failures don't change the odds of the next trial.
cards.note: The only memoryless discrete distribution — the exponential's discrete twin.

cards.q: Time between consecutive customer arrivals, given a Poisson process.
cards.note: Waiting time between events in a Poisson process; memoryless.

cards.q: Heights of adults — clustered around a centre with symmetric spread.
cards.note: Many small additive factors → Central Limit Theorem.

cards.q: A random number equally likely anywhere in [0, 1].
cards.note: Flat density: no value in the range is favoured over another.

cards.q: Your belief about an unknown coin's bias p, as a distribution on [0, 1].
cards.note: Lives on [0, 1], so it's the natural model for an unknown probability.

cards.q: Centre and spread of a Normal
cards.a: μ centres the bell; σ sets its width.
cards.note: 68% of the mass lands within 1σ of μ. Bigger σ = more spread.

cards.q: Memoryless property (exponential / Poisson)
cards.a: Past elapsed time doesn't change future odds.
cards.note: Waited 30 min for a bus? The next 10 min are no more likely than before.

cards.q: Mean of an Exponential with rate λ
cards.note: Higher rate → events closer together → shorter average wait.

cards.q: CDF of an Exponential with rate λ
cards.note: As x → ∞ it approaches 1 — eventually the event happens.

cards.q: PDF vs CDF — what's the difference?
cards.a: PDF = density; CDF = accumulated P(X ≤ x).
cards.note: Area under the PDF is probability; the CDF is that area running left to right.

cards.q: "Is the Normal the right default for most real-world data?"
cards.note: Real data is often skewed, heavy-tailed, or multimodal. Use Normal with CLT or symmetry evidence.

cards.q: "A PDF is a probability, so it can't exceed 1 — right?"
cards.note: Only the area integrates to 1. A narrow Uniform on [0, 0.5] has height 2.

cards.q: What is a Beta(1, 1) distribution?
cards.a: The Uniform on [0, 1] — a flat prior.
cards.note: Every bias equally plausible: 'no prior knowledge' about p.

cards.q: The 68–95–99.7 rule for a Normal
cards.note: A fast sanity check for how extreme a value is.

cards.q: Standard deviation vs variance
cards.a: σ = √Var. σ is in the data's own units.
cards.note: Variance is in squared units; σ is what you compare to the mean.

cards.q: Bayes' theorem
cards.note: Likelihood × Prior / Evidence. Rearranges belief in light of new data.

cards.q: The prior in Bayesian inference
cards.a: Your belief before seeing the data.
cards.note: Weak prior → let data dominate; strong prior → hard to shift.

cards.q: The posterior in Bayesian inference
cards.a: Your updated belief after seeing the data.
cards.note: Combines prior and likelihood; used for prediction and inference.

cards.q: The likelihood in Bayes' theorem
cards.a: How well each hypothesis explains the observed data.
cards.note: P(data | hypothesis) — read as a function of the hypothesis, not the data.

cards.q: Estimate a coin's p from 7 heads in 10 flips, with no prior belief.
cards.a: Beta prior (Beta(1,1)), update to a posterior.
cards.note: Prior + observed data → posterior over p.

cards.q: "Uniform prior — so Bayesian and frequentist answers must match?"
cards.a: Often close for large samples, not identical in principle.
cards.note: The prior always shapes the posterior, even when weak. Different philosophies.

cards.q: What is a conjugate prior?
cards.a: A prior whose posterior stays in the same family.
cards.note: Beta prior + Binomial data → Beta posterior. Keeps updating algebraically clean.

cards.q: Beta(α, β) prior + h heads, t tails (Binomial). Posterior?
cards.note: Just add successes to α and failures to β. The conjugate-update shortcut.

cards.q: "Strong prior, only a little data — what wins?"
cards.note: Data has to be plentiful or surprising to move a confident prior.

cards.q: The evidence / marginal P(B) in Bayes' theorem
cards.a: A normalizing constant so the posterior sums to 1.
cards.note: Same for every hypothesis, so it doesn't change which one wins — only the scale.

cards.q: Buses arriving at a stop: rare, independent, at a constant average rate.
cards.note: Counts are Poisson; gaps between arrivals are Exponential.

cards.q: In a rate-λ process, the number of events in time t is…
cards.note: Rate and time scale together: λ = 3/hr, t = 2 hr → Poisson(6).

cards.q: In a rate-λ process, the time between events is…
cards.note: The count/wait duality: Poisson counts, Exponential gaps.

cards.q: Probability of zero events in time t
Why does the memoryless property matter here?
cards.a: The wait to the next event doesn't age.
cards.note: Elapsed waiting carries no information about how much longer you'll wait.

cards.q: "I've waited ages — isn't the next bus 'due' now?"
cards.note: The remaining wait has the same distribution it had when you arrived.

cards.q: The rate λ of a Poisson process
cards.a: Events per unit time; expected count scales as λt.
cards.note: Doubling the window doubles the expected number of events.

cards.q: Merge two independent Poisson processes, rates λ₁ and λ₂.
cards.a: A Poisson process with rate λ₁ + λ₂.
cards.note: Superposition: pooled arrivals are still Poisson, rates add.

cards.q: What does independence of A and B mean?
cards.a: Knowing B tells you nothing about A.
cards.note: The joint probability factorises into the product of the two.

cards.q: Definition of conditional probability
cards.note: Restrict the world to B, then ask how much of it is also A.

cards.q: "Mutually exclusive events are independent — right?"
cards.note: If A rules out B, then knowing A happened tells you B didn't. Opposite of independent.

cards.q: What is the expected value of a random variable?
cards.a: Its long-run average, Σ x · P(x).
cards.note: A probability-weighted mean — not necessarily a value X can actually take.

cards.q: The complement rule
cards.note: Often far easier to compute P(at least one) as 1 − P(none).

cards.q: When do you add probabilities vs multiply them?
cards.a: OR adds (minus overlap); AND multiplies (if independent).
cards.note: P(A∪B) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B).  P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B) only when independent.
